paras: The attempted lynching of Willie and Otho Green was a pair of mob actions in western Virginia in July and August 1903, in which armed men tried to seize two Black prisoners accused of shooting Harry Rudisill, first by firing into a train near Clifton Forge and then by threatening the jail at Covington. No one was hurt, and troops escorted the two men by special train to Lynchburg and then to Bedford City. Wire services carried the train shooting nationally; the Covington standoff was reported mainly in Virginia.

Willie and Otho Green, also called Will and Otto, were accused of shooting Rudisill on a Chesapeake and Ohio excursion train at Abert station, Bedford County, on Wednesday night, July 29. They told reporters they were half brothers aged eighteen and twenty-four working as farm laborers at Balcony Falls. After their arrest they were brought to Clifton Forge on Thursday for identification, but Rudisill had just been operated on and could not see them. Fearing a mob, officials put them aboard train No. 1 for the Covington jail.

At about 9:25 p.m., half a mile west of Clifton Forge, men waving lights flagged the train to a stop. The crowd, put at one to two hundred men, held the engineer under revolvers and, finding the doors locked by Conductor Jack Hall, fired into the smoking car where the prisoners were guarded. When his guards left to join the shooting, the engineer opened the throttle, and the train reached Covington with no one hurt.

On Saturday, August 1, a Clifton Forge correspondent reported a mob of four hundred or more assembling and wrote that "threats of lynching are heard on every side." At Covington, Deputy Sheriff A. C. Sizer armed fifteen or twenty men to guard the jail and at 10:25 p.m. called out the Clifton Forge Rifles, who arrived before midnight. Shortly before, the old hose-house near the jail caught fire, which many residents believed the mob had set as a diversion, but no attempt was made to force the jail.

Sheriff F. M. Turner sent the prisoners and troops on a special train that ran through Clifton Forge without stopping early Sunday. At Lynchburg the forty-two soldiers marched the handcuffed men to jail, and that afternoon Bedford County's sheriff took them to Bedford City.

Covington's citizens were reported unanimous in commending Sizer. Railroad and federal detectives were sent to Clifton Forge to identify the men who stopped the train, whose mail car had been hit, but no arrests appear in the coverage. No report of the Greens' trial was found.

The train hold-up drew the widest coverage, starting with the Huntington Advertiser's same-day story and a closely matching Associated Press dispatch. Papers ran it as "MOB FIRE ON TRAIN" (Richmond Times-Dispatch), "SEEKING NEGROES' LIVES" (Raleigh News & Observer) and "STORMING A TRAIN" (Evening Star). A shorter second wire, headed "MOB TRIES TO LYNCH 2 NEGROES" in Providence, said the prisoners had fatally shot a brakeman. These stories did not name the prisoners and centered on the train crew; one Times-Dispatch headline read "ENGINEER FOILED PLAN."

The Covington standoff appeared mainly in Times-Dispatch specials headed "A LYNCHING IS FEARED" and "Military Guard Prevented the Lynching of Willie and Otho Green." The same paper praised the officials who protected the prisoners, yet its digest called the Greens the "supposed slayers" of a man still alive. A Lynchburg wire on their removal ran in the New-York Tribune as "KEEP NEGROES MOVING," and the Pocahontas Times called the train episode an "atempted lynching party."

The only Black-press report found was a front-page Savannah Tribune story of August 8, "MOB HELD UP TRAIN," which reprinted the Associated Press account without comment and did not report the Covington standoff.

The Huntington Advertiser, the Associated Press and the Times-Dispatch placed the train hold-up on Thursday night, July 30; the Lynchburg wire, the Free Lance and the Savannah Tribune said Friday, and the Pocahontas Times Wednesday. The Huntington report, printed the day after the hold-up, is the earliest.
The Free Lance, following the second wire, said the prisoners were charged with fatally shooting a brakeman named Will Rambow, while Virginia reports named Rudisill as the wounded man.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Willie and Otho Green
bases: Armed crowds twice tried to take two accused Black prisoners from custody to lynch them, firing into the train carrying them and then threatening the Covington jail (A1, A2, A9, A16).

A mob of one to two hundred men, acting without authority over the shooting of Harry Rudisill, fired into the prisoners' car and later threatened the jail, but no one was killed or injured (A1, A2, A16).

The train hold-up is reported independently by the Huntington Advertiser, two wire services and a West Virginia weekly, and the Covington threat by separate Times-Dispatch correspondents in Clifton Forge, Covington and Lynchburg (A1, A2, A3, A9, A16, A20).

accounts.label: Huntington wire (AP) and local report
accounts.gist: A mob of 100-200 flagged train No. 1 near Clifton Forge, held the engineer at gunpoint and fired over a hundred shots into the smoker carrying two prisoners; the engineer escaped and the men were jailed at Covington.

accounts.label: Second wire
accounts.gist: Two hundred armed men stopped the fast mail with red lanterns and fired fifty shots into the prisoners' coach; the prisoners were charged with fatally shooting a brakeman.

accounts.label: Clifton Forge correspondent
accounts.gist: A mob of four hundred or more was assembling amid lynching threats, and the Rifles were called to Covington.

accounts.label: Covington correspondent
accounts.gist: The deputy sheriff's armed guard and the Rifles held the jail; a hose-house fire was thought a diversion, but no attempt was made on the jail and strangers only gathered in small groups.

accounts.label: Judge George K. Anderson
accounts.gist: The prisoners were taken to Clifton Forge for an identification Rudisill could not make, the mob shot out the train's windows, and a 2 a.m. special train ran them through Clifton Forge without stopping.

framing.detail: Wire headlines such as 'MOB FIRE ON TRAIN' and 'Make Desperate Effort to Lynch Two Negroes' told the hold-up as a train drama in which the engineer 'FOILED PLAN'.

Times-Dispatch specials ('A LYNCHING IS FEARED', 'Military Guard Prevented the Lynching') praised the deputy sheriff's 'firm stand', while its digest called the prisoners the 'supposed slayers' of a man still alive.
The Evening Star and papers in Raleigh, Providence, Perth Amboy, Waterbury and Savannah ran the wire texts under headlines such as 'STORMING A TRAIN' and 'MOB TRIES TO LYNCH 2 NEGROES'.
The Savannah Tribune ran the AP hold-up text on its front page as 'MOB HELD UP TRAIN / USED MUCH AMMUNITION', without comment.

conflicts.note: The Huntington Advertiser of July 31 said 'last night' and the train reached Huntington that morning; with Judge Anderson's and the Lynchburg correspondent's statement that the prisoners went to Clifton Forge on Thursday, this same-day report is the best evidence. The Free Lance gives both Thursday and Friday.

Black ('negro prisoners'; one described as a light mulatto)
Episode begins with the train hold-up on the night of July 30 and ends with removal of the prisoners early August 2; the Covington threat was August 1
No seizure and no siege of the jail; the mob stopped the train and fired into the prisoners' car (shooting, property damage), then threatened the jail with an armed gathering
Train attack near Clifton Forge; threatened jail attack at Covington
